rationale: Bounded pass. Of the report's candidates, three primaries were actually shown to me: Heckenberger et al. 2008 (full text via the Socioambiental mirror), Prümers et al. 2022 (full text via PMC), and the Bush et al. 2021 supplementary materials (CentAUR) — plus two institutional releases (Bonn 2022, Reading/phys.org 2021). The archive.org fetch for Medina 1894 returned only the catalog page, so every Introducción observation in F1 is blocked (the report's quotations are not in front of me); I add the URL to SRC-CARVAJAL-1542 as a correction because the report reached the edition there. Iriarte 2020 (bot page), Rostain 2024 (403), and the Neves chapter (bot page) are blocked. The Bush 2021 main-text finding is entered only as the Reading release reports it, as a linked alternative to AMZ-C015, never merged; the primary stays blocked with a route. Casarabe's AD 500–1400 span enters from the primary, with the 4,500 vs 16,000 km² discrepancy between paper and release recorded, not resolved. The Xingu '1770' correction fails: the shown source neither states nor contradicts it. No edition proposed: the load-bearing competitor (pre-European reforestation) is verified only at secondary level.

sources.title: Pre-Columbian Urbanism, Anthropogenic Landscapes, and the Future of the Amazon
reliabilityNotes: Read from a PDF mirror at acervo.socioambiental.org; the publisher page (doi.org) returned HTTP 403. Mirror page [p. 1] begins with the tail of an unrelated preceding article; mirror [p. 1]–[p. 4] correspond to journal pp. 1214–1217.
Primary anchor for the Upper Xingu material; AMZ-E019 currently rests on a news feature (SRC-SCIENCE-XINGU-2024). This paper gives no '1770' terminus.
Population figures are the authors' estimates from ethnographic conversion (walled towns 800–1000+, villages 250±100 persons), stated as conservative (note 25).

sources.title: Lidar reveals pre-Hispanic low-density urbanism in the Bolivian Amazon
reliabilityNotes: Peer-reviewed article, Nature 606:325–328 (2022), open access CC BY 4.0; read via the PMC copy (PMC9177426) because nature.com was not reached.
Chronology rests on 144 radiocarbon dates from a limited number of sites; stratigraphic information from only four sites (Methods).
States the Casarabe culture area 'as far as known today' as ~4,500 km²; the University of Bonn release for the same paper says ~16,000 km² — discrepancy recorded, not resolved.

Funded by the German Archaeological Institute; lidar sensor from ERC-PAST (J. Iriarte). Overlaps in authorship with Iriarte 2020 and with SRC-LOMBARDO-2025's research community; not independent of Prestes-Carneiro 2019 (shared authors Prümers, Jaimes Betancourt).

sources.title: Early urbanism found in the Amazon (University of Bonn press release on Prümers et al. 2022)
reliabilityNotes: Institutional press release (25 May 2022); secondary to SRC-PRUMERS-2022 and not independent of it.

Gives the Casarabe culture area as 'around 16,000 square kilometers', which conflicts with the paper's ~4,500 km²; use only for the discrepancy and for author statements not in the paper (e.g., 'not yet possible to estimate how many people lived there').

sources.title: Widespread reforestation before European influence on Amazonia
reliabilityNotes: ONLY the Supplementary Materials (accepted version, CentAUR repository) were shown to me; the main text with the headline finding was not retrieved. Evidence records here are limited to the methods and dataset description.
Shares authors (McMichael, Maezumi) with SRC-MCMICHAEL-2017, SRC-MCMICHAEL-2025 and the sparse-western-Amazonia research group; not independent of those records.
Charcoal data pooled from many investigators without a standardized protocol; standardized post hoc as a Charcoal Index (SI p. 4–5).

sources.title: Pre-Columbus climate change may have caused Amazon population decline (University of Reading release on Bush et al. 2021, via phys.org)
reliabilityNotes: Institutional press release republished by phys.org (24 May 2021); secondary to SRC-BUSH-2021 and not independent of it.

Used only until the Science main text is read; its statements of the finding (regrowth for 'over 800 years', management peak 'around 1200 AD', no Orbis Spike link) must be confirmed against the paper.
The climate-change driver is presented as a co-author's suggestion ('raises the possibility'), not a demonstrated result.

evidence.title: Heckenberger 2008: Upper Xingu galactic clusters ~750–450 BP, depopulation only after ~500–400 BP, layouts matching contemporary villages
evidence.sourceStatement: The source states that its survey and excavations focused on galactic clusters dated ~750 to 450 yr B.P., and that "After ~500 to 400 yr B.P., early European colonialism resulted in" substantial depopulation and forest expansion; it identifies 28 prehistoric residential sites, notes that "Smaller nonwalled plaza villages are similar in size and form to larger contemporary" villages, and that the relation of sites X6 and X18 to X13 is "similar to the orientation of high-ranking houses in the contemporary Kuikuro village".
evidence.editorInference: Primary anchor for the Xingu clause of AMZ-C011, which currently rests on a news feature (AMZ-E019). It supports occupation to the contact horizon and layout continuity. It does NOT state the 'ca. 1770' terminus in AMZ-C011; that figure must be sourced elsewhere (see disposition).
evidence.exactLocator: [p. 2] (journal p. 1215) and [p. 3] (journal p. 1216), PDF mirror at acervo.socioambiental.org
limitations: Terminus given only as 'after ~500 to 400 yr B.P.'; no calendar date for final abandonment.
Radiocarbon dates concentrate on earthwork construction (~750–700 BP); the occupation end is inferred, not dated (note 16).

evidence.title: Heckenberger 2008: regional population estimated at ≥50,000 from ethnographic conversion, stated as conservative
evidence.sourceStatement: The source states that the "regional peer polity was composed of 15 or more clusters" across ≥20,000 km², and "We estimate a regional population of" ≥50,000 (>2.5 persons/km²); note 25 says "We consider these conservative estimates", expecting more clusters in uninvestigated areas. Walled towns are assigned 800–1000 or more persons "as known ethnographically from adjacent areas" and villages 250 ± 100.
evidence.editorInference: Supports the existence of the estimate as the authors' figure. The estimate depends on cluster count, contemporaneity, and ethnographic persons-per-settlement conversions — the same assumption family flagged for AMZ-C005, AMZ-C006, AMZ-C012.
evidence.exactLocator: [p. 3] (journal p. 1216) and [p. 4] note 25 (journal p. 1217), PDF mirror
limitations: Only two clusters were surveyed; the ≥15-cluster regional figure is extrapolated from spacing of known centres and indigenous knowledge (notes 25, 48).

evidence.title: Heckenberger 2008: a mosaic of islands of acute human influence and less affected forest tracts
evidence.sourceStatement: The source states that mosaic landscapes "alternated between areas or islands of acute human influence" (settlements, roads, agricultural countryside) and less affected areas between settlements and particularly between clusters, "characterized by large tracts of high forest".
evidence.editorInference: A regional-scale statement of the heterogeneity pattern AMZ-C016 asserts basin-wide. Moderate: one region, and the authors' own interpretive synthesis.
limitations: Single region (Upper Xingu); the paper's inference of land-use zones is modeled on contemporary Kuikuro practice.

evidence.title: Prümers 2022: the Casarabe culture is dated ca. AD 500–1400
evidence.sourceStatement: The source dates the "Casarabe culture (around ad 500 to ad 1400)" on the basis of 144 radiocarbon dates, of which 94 come from the PABAM sites Mendoza and Salvatierra, with Bayesian modelling in OxCal (Methods).
evidence.editorInference: Casarabe's end therefore predates Orellana by roughly 140 years; this bears on how AMZ-C007 can be used in the founding question (see AMZ-E027).
evidence.exactLocator: Abstract and Main; Methods, 'Radiocarbon dating' — via open-access PMC copy (PMC9177426)
limitations: Stratigraphic control from only four sites; 22 dates from Chocolatelito could not be integrated; two dates ca. AD 0–220 are flagged by the authors as unusually early.

evidence.title: Prümers 2022: the year-round maize agriculturalists of Casarabe belong to a culture that ended ca. AD 1400
evidence.sourceStatement: The source states that monumental sites were "inhabited throughout the year by agriculturalists who cultivated a diversity of crops", with maize as primary staple, and dates the culture to around AD 500 to AD 1400.
evidence.editorInference: Confirms the subsistence picture of AMZ-C007 while bounding it in time: the best-documented engineered-subsistence case is not contact-era archaeology. This qualifies the use of AMZ-C007 as an answer to what Carvajal's populations 'could have eaten', without denying the claim.
evidence.exactLocator: Main, first paragraph — via open-access PMC copy
limitations: Subsistence statements cite earlier excavation and bioarchaeology (refs 10–12, 20–23), not new data in this paper.

evidence.title: Prümers 2022: lidar reveals two >100 ha sites in a four-tiered settlement system
evidence.sourceStatement: The source reports lidar of 204 km² revealing Cotoca (147 ha) and Landívar (315 ha) "in a dense four-tiered settlement system", with stepped platforms, U-shaped structures, conical pyramids up to 22 m, concentric polygonal enclosures, radiating causeways and "Massive water-management infrastructure, composed of canals and reservoirs"; "A 7-km canal brought water from Laguna San José to Cotoca".
evidence.exactLocator: Abstract; 'Large settlement sites'; 'Low-density urbanism of the Casarabe culture' — via open-access PMC copy
limitations: Lidar covered six unconnected areas totalling ~200 km² selected for known concentrations of major settlements.

evidence.title: Prümers 2022 vs Bonn release: Casarabe culture area stated as ~4,500 km² in the paper, ~16,000 km² in the release
evidence.sourceStatement: The release states the Casarabe culture "according to current knowledge, extended over a region of around 16,000 square kilometers"; the paper (SRC-PRUMERS-2022) states "The Casarabe culture area, as far as known today, spans approximately" 4,500 km².
evidence.editorInference: The two figures from the same team in the same month differ by a factor of ~3.5; I cannot reconcile them from the shown texts. The peer-reviewed figure should be preferred until the discrepancy is explained (possibly different definitions of 'culture area' vs region of influence).
evidence.exactLocator: Bonn release, paragraph beginning 'This indicated a relatively dense settlement'; PMC copy of the paper, Abstract
limitations: Press release; may paraphrase a broader regional extent than the paper's documented settlement area.

evidence.title: Prümers 2022: authors declare western-Amazonia sparse-population arguments 'put to rest'
evidence.sourceStatement: The source's Conclusions state: "Our results put to rest arguments that western Amazonia was sparsely populated" in pre-Hispanic times, citing McMichael et al. 2012.
evidence.editorInference: Rhetorical rather than evidential against AMZ-C014: the Llanos de Mojos is a seasonally flooded savannah with Andean-derived soils, not the terra-firme forest the phytolith synthesis samples. Low diagnosticity; recorded because it is a direct published rejoinder from a primary source.
limitations: The 'western Amazonia' targeted is McMichael 2012's; the Casarabe area is at the southwestern savannah fringe, environmentally distinct from most sampled terra-firme sites.

evidence.title: Bush 2021 SI: 39 lake-sediment pollen and charcoal records, Cecropia as abandonment indicator, Great Dying window 1550–1750
evidence.sourceStatement: The supplementary materials state the authors "compiled fossil pollen and charcoal data from 39 lake-sediment records" in Amazonia sensu stricto, each with a minimum of six pollen samples within the last 2000 years; Cecropia is treated as "an indicator of site abandonment and early successional forest regrowth"; nine high-resolution sites show forest-pollen change "before, during, and after the Great Dying period (1550-1750)".
evidence.editorInference: Supports only the dataset/method description. The headline result (timing of regrowth) is not in the shown text.
evidence.exactLocator: [p. 4]–[p. 5] (SI pp. 2–3), accepted-version supplementary PDF via CentAUR (centaur.reading.ac.uk/97776)
limitations: Supplementary materials only; main text unread.
Charcoal not collected under a standardized protocol; standardized post hoc.

evidence.title: Reading release: pollen records indicate regrowth began >800 years ago at many sites, a pre-European decline
evidence.sourceStatement: The release states that analysis of fossil pollen and charcoal revealed that "many previously deforested lands have been recovering for over 800 years", rather than 400, "indicating a pre-European population decline"; that "human management of the rainforest may have peaked around 1200 AD"; and quotes co-author Mayle that the analysis raises the possibility that "climate change caused the decline of some Amazonian societies several centuries before" Europeans arrived.
evidence.editorInference: Secondary statement of a primary finding I have not read; weak until the Science main text is opened. The climate driver is offered as a possibility, not a result.
limitations: Does not say which of the 39 sites show early regrowth or whether any lie on Carvajal's main-stem corridor.

evidence.title: Reading release: pre-European reforestation as a competing account of the pre-contact trajectory
evidence.sourceStatement: The release reports that the pollen and charcoal analysis "challenges the prior assumption that the largest population decrease" began only after European contact, with regrowth at some sites beginning over 800 years ago.
evidence.editorInference: The radiocarbon SPD proxy (SRC-ARROYOKALIN-2021) reads growth to carrying capacity before contact; the pollen proxy as reported here reads abandonment beginning ca. 1200 CE at many sites. The two proxies disagree; this record limits AMZ-C015 without refuting it. Strength weak because secondary; AMZ-C015's provisional verdict already accommodates it.
limitations: Secondary; primary main text not read.

evidence.title: Reading release: no evidence the Orbis Spike was caused by Amazonian reforestation
evidence.sourceStatement: The release states the team found "no evidence that the Orbis Spike was caused by Amazonian reforestation".
evidence.editorInference: Bears on collapse mechanisms only indirectly (post-contact forest regrowth as carbon sink). Low diagnosticity for the founding question.
limitations: Secondary; a negative result reported without the underlying figures.

research.title: Two proxies, one trajectory: map the 39 Bush et al. pollen records against Carvajal's corridor and the radiocarbon SPD
research.summary: Open Bush et al. 2021 (Science 372:484–487) in full with Database S1; tabulate for each of the 39 lakes its location, its onset of forest-pollen recovery, and whether it lies on the main-stem/major-tributary corridors Carvajal described or in interfluves and southern savannas. Then compare against the regional breakdown of the summed radiocarbon distribution in SRC-ARROYOKALIN-2021 to determine whether the disagreement between proxies is basin-wide or a matter of where each samples.
research.informationGain: Settles whether the pre-European abandonment signal is concentrated off Carvajal's corridor (leaving AMZ-C015 and the 'died between the visits' reading intact for the main river) or extends to riverine sites (which would force a mixed pre- and post-contact collapse account into the edition).

research.title: Which Aquiry earthworks postdate AD 1400? Separating the geoglyph peak from the Mound Village horizon in the 2026 tally
research.summary: Re-read SRC-PARSSINEN-2026 and its supplement to classify the 432 documented earthworks by type and by any available dates; determine whether Mound Villages (Iriarte et al. 2020: ~AD 1000–1650) are counted among them and how many carry dates after AD 1400. Obtain Iriarte et al. 2020 (JCAA 3(1), doi:10.5334/jcaa.45) from the open PDF to fix the type chronology.
research.informationGain: Determines whether southwestern Amazonia contributes any contact-horizon evidence to the founding question or only an AD 100–300 demonstration of environmental capacity, and refines what fraction of the 24,000–30,000 projection belongs to which era.
